children: Global trade in goods is set for continued growth despite higher U.S. tariffs and uncertainty caused by the conflict in the Middle East, according to a leading indicator compiled by the World Trade Organization.

The Geneva-based body that mediates trade disputes Wednesday said its Trade Barometer rose to 102.0 in July from 101.7 in April. A reading above 100 indicates exports and imports are rising at a faster pace than the average rate recorded over recent decades.

"Strong demand for electronic components and other inputs associated with investment in artificial intelligence continues to support trade, helping to offset the negative effects of conflict in the Middle East and ongoing uncertainty surrounding trade policies," the WTO said.
In 2025, the AI investment boom drove trade flows to levels that were well above those anticipated by most economists when President Trump announced a big rise in tariffs in early April.

That boost has continued this year, with the volumes of goods crossing national borders jumping again in the first three months of the year. While the start of the conflict between the U.S. and Iran led to a fall in trade flows during March, they have since rebounded, and the WTO said its indicator suggests that "trade growth continues to pick up in the third quarter of 2026."
The trade body's barometer is composed of a number of measures that have a history of pointing to changes in the volume of trade flows.

The WTO said the electronic components measure produced the highest reading at 104.9, but a measure of export orders based on surveys of purchasing managers had also strengthened, "pointing to stronger goods trade growth in the months ahead."
The only component showing signs of weakness was the measure for container shipping, which fell slightly below trend.
U.S. trade policy and the duration of the war remain key uncertainties for those attempting to forecast world trade flows.

President Trump on Tuesday signed orders to ban the importation of many dairy products, alcoholic beverages and motorcycles from Canada, having previously announced tariffs of 50% on imports of a range of products from the country.
